content.title: About
content.content: Horseradish sauce is made from fresh horseradish root, vinegar, salt and sometimes sugar, cream or mustard. It has a sharp, pungent flavor and a distinctive aroma that intensifies with storage. The sauce is commonly used as a condiment for meat, fish, vegetables and as an ingredient in salad dressings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Horseradish is one of the spiciest vegetables; its heat comes from glucosinolates that convert to mustard oil when the root is grated.
Traditional horseradish sauce originated in medieval Europe as a way to preserve the root’s flavor.
In Russia, horseradish sauce is often served with cold appetizers such as herring under a fur coat and boiled eggs.
The combination of horseradish and vinegar extends the sauce’s shelf life to several months.
In Japan a similar condiment called wasabi is made from a different plant – the wasabi rhizome.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Glucosinolates in horseradish have antioxidant properties that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The spiciness stimulates gastric juice production, aiding digestion.

items.title: Anti‑inflammatory effects
items.content: Research indicates horseradish compounds may reduce inflammation in the body.

items.title: May help regulate blood sugar
items.content: Some studies link horseradish consumption with improved glycemic control.

items.title: Boosts immunity
items.content: Vitamin C and other phytochemicals in horseradish support the immune system.

items.title: Mucous membrane irritation
items.content: The strong heat can cause burning sensations in the mouth, stomach or intestines for sensitive individuals.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some people may experience allergic reactions to horseradish or its components.

items.title: Interaction with medications
items.content: Large amounts of horseradish may enhance the effect of anticoagulants, so caution is advised for those on blood thinners.

items.title: Stomach issues
items.content: People with ulcers or gastritis should limit consumption of very spicy horseradish sauce.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve horseradish sauce in small amounts as a condiment for meat, fish, boiled vegetables, or mix it into mayonnaise or sour cream for a milder flavor. It also works well in marinades and dressings.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the sauce in a tightly sealed jar in the refrigerator. Properly stored, it retains its flavor and aroma for 3–4 months. Discard if the smell changes or mold appears.
